doc.title: Bob Stewart interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006

title: The four-valve tuba
summary: He explains what a fourth valve does for low register tuning and fingering.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: Wow. I noticed you play a four valver?
How does that make a difference?

Well that fourth valve, there are some flugelhorns that are made with four valves — Miraphone, the tuba manufacturer makes a flugelhorn, and there are probably some other manufacturers. Jimmy Owens plays a flugelhorn with four valves and there are a couple of other people. I think Earl Gardner, no maybe not Earl Gardner, somebody else plays the four valve, but Jimmy Owens definitely does. What it does is like on trumpet the lowest note is F sharp, all three valves down. And then if you’ve got good chops you kind of play a pedal — I’m talking the trumpet pitch now — a pedal C. But with that fourth valve it allows you to play all the notes between that low F sharp and the C in tune. So F sharp, low F would be one and four, the low E would be the one, two and four or two three and four, low E flat is one, three and four, low D is all four down, and then you get the pedal C. But you can play them all, they’re all built on the horn with that fourth valve.
It also is a substitute for one and three. Anything you can play one and three you can play with the fourth valve.
